title: Therapy, Panic Attacks and the Pahwas: 'Perfect Family' Lands on SonyLIV and Holds Up a Mirror
excerpt: Pankaj Tripathi's debut as a producer puts a flawless-looking Delhi household in mandatory therapy with Neha Dhupia — and the result is the most honest family drama of the year.
body:
There's a particular kind of Indian household that looks immaculate in the WhatsApp display picture and runs on quiet warfare behind the door. **Perfect Family**, which dropped on **SonyLIV** on June 26, walks straight into that house, sits down at the dining table, and refuses to leave until everyone says the thing they've been swallowing for years.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=2UbTyjv01ro</youtube>

It opens, fittingly, with a fight about a party theme. The **Karkarias** — a Delhi family that photographs beautifully — are bickering over decorations when the cracks start to show. Patriarch **Somnath** (a wonderfully blustery **Manoj Pahwa**) and his son **Vishnu** (**Gulshan Devaiah**, all simmering resentment) circle each other like two men who've rehearsed this argument a thousand times. Matriarch **Kamla** (**Seema Pahwa**) keeps the peace by pretending there's peace to keep. And then 12-year-old **Daani**, the youngest, has a panic attack at school — and the whole carefully maintained facade comes down.

The school's prescription is the engine of the show: mandatory family therapy. Enter **Neha Dhupia** as **Megha**, the psychotherapist tasked with handing this family a "mental fitness certificate" they very much do not deserve yet. What follows across eight episodes is part comedy, part slow excavation — every session prying loose another buried grievance, another generational wound, another thing nobody was supposed to say out loud.

> "The beauty of this show lies in its honesty. It doesn't try to give easy answers or perfect characters. It simply holds up a mirror to family dynamics in a very raw and relatable way." — Neha Dhupia

What makes **Perfect Family** worth your weekend is the cast, and specifically the **Manoj Pahwa–Seema Pahwa** pairing — two of the finest character actors working in Hindi cinema, finally handed the center of the frame instead of the margins. Critics noticed. *The Indian Express* gave it 3.5/5, calling it "beautifully relatable" and praising how it introduces therapy without ever turning preachy. *India Today* singled out the Pahwas and noted the show "resists the glossy facade" of the typical family drama. *Hindustan Times* gave three stars and a warmer verdict — "a sincere look at therapy and trauma" — while gently dinging the overuse of flashbacks. *Scroll.in* summed it up best: "full of home truths about family relationships."

It's also a notable debut on two fronts. **Perfect Family** marks **Pankaj Tripathi**'s first outing as a producer — yes, the *Mirzapur* and *Gangs of Wasseypur* legend is now backing stories rather than just stealing scenes in them — co-produced by Ajay Rai's JAR Pictures. Created by **Palak Bhambri** and directed by **Sachin Pathak**, the series had an unusual first life: it premiered on YouTube in late 2025 on a pay-per-view model, with the first two episodes free and the rest behind a one-time payment. The SonyLIV move is its proper streaming arrival — the version with a marketing push and a subscription audience.

And here's why it matters beyond the metro multiplex crowd. Therapy, mental health, generational silence — these are precisely the subjects the diaspora wrestles with in its own living rooms, often without a vocabulary for them. A show that frames a panic attack not as shame but as the moment a family finally gets honest is doing quiet, useful work. It's *Kabhi Khushi Kabhie Gham* with the gloss scraped off and a therapist in the room.

**Where to watch:** **Perfect Family** is streaming exclusively on **SonyLIV**, which is available to diaspora viewers in the US, UK, Canada, and beyond via international subscription plans (often bundled or sold standalone outside India). All eight episodes are live, so this is a one-sitting binge if your household can handle that much honesty in a single weekend. The series runs in Hindi.

The take: this isn't a flashy release, and it won't trend the way a ₹350-crore spy film does. But it's the kind of show that lingers — the one that makes you text your mother afterward, or sit a little longer at your own dining table. In a streaming landscape addicted to crime, gore, and spectacle, a small, sharp, beautifully acted drama about a family learning to talk to each other is its own kind of radical. Devaiah and the Pahwas alone make it a must-watch. Just maybe don't watch it with the relatives you're currently not speaking to.
